answer: Agents can require each participant to lock a scarce, slashable stake before it earns influence: a jade-market kernel might accept only signed actions routed through a bridge contract that records deposits and penalties. If identities coordinate to fake broad support, the protocol can slash stake tied to provably conflicting actions, so creating more names does not multiply voting power. The attacker must acquire and lock real capital, then risks losing it, making a Sybil campaign costly rather than free.
